newsitem.title: USA: Clinton expands pollution disclosure program.
newsitem.headline: Clinton expands pollution disclosure program.

text.p: In observance of Earth Day, President Bill Clinton on Tuesday said he was increasing by 30 percent the number of industrial firms that must publicly report on the toxic chemicals they emit.

Clinton, who spoke on environmental issues shortly before leaving to survey the wreckage from massive floods in North Dakota, also said the nation must step up research on whether industrial pollution is contributing to catastrophic weather events.

"We have to find the best scientific evidence we have and we have to keep searching for the answers to this," he said. "I think every American has noticed a substantial increase in the last few years of the kind of thing we are going to see in North Dakota today."
The United States is negotiating with other industrialised countries to reduce pollution from burning fossil fuels that scientists say traps heat in the atmosphere and changes the world's climate.

Clinton's action to expand reporting on industries' emissions of toxic chemicals, which carries out a pledge announced by Vice President Al Gore last June, added seven new industry categories that must reveal their chemical releases.
It added 6,100 facilities that must disclose emissions of dangerous chemicals under the Toxic Release Inventory programme and raised the total number that must report to 31,000.
"By expanding community right-to-know, we are giving Americans a powerful, very powerful early-warning system to keep their children safe from toxic pollution," Clinton said.

"This law tells citizens exactly what substances are being released into their neighbourhoods. In the decade it's been on the books citizens have joined with government and industry to reduce the release of toxic chemicals by 43 percent," he said.

The rule adds metal and coal mining, electric utilities, commercial hazardous waste treatment, petroleum bulk terminals, chemical wholesalers and solvent recovery services to the 20 other categories of industries that must report. In addition, 700 chemical manufacturing facilities that already must participate in the programme will have to provide more information on the pollution they produce.

Clinton spoke as environmentalists across the country marked the 27th Earth Day with speeches, concerts, tree plantings and other events. In Washington, Gore helped clean up the Anacostia River, Attorney General Janet Reno helped in a community cleanup and Secretary of State Madeleine Albright released a report on U.S. progress in "environmental diplomacy."

Environmentalists praise the Toxic Release Inventory programme as an important tool to discourage industries from polluting and inform communities of risks they face, but industries slam it as costly, burdensome government intrusion.

"We were not happy to hear the announcement that we were included. Based on the cost of compliance of our members and the minimal releases, we thought there was no justification to include us," a spokesman for the National Association of Chemical Distributors said.

"We don't think it provides accurate information to the public. It's certainly not risk-related information," a counsel for the National Mining Association, which represents the coal and metal mining industries, said.
Carolyn Hartmann, of the U.S. Public Interest Research Group, said the new rule "fills some important gaps in the public's right to know, but we still have a long way to go."

She said more steps should be taken to inform the public on toxic chemicals they may be exposed to in the workplace and through consumer products. She also said industries should report on chemicals that are highly toxic in very small quantities, such as heavy metals and dioxins.
